title: Market Research
text:
Global equities have staged a resilient rebound over the last three months, driven by a “Goldilocks” macro backdrop where cooling inflation and robust corporate earnings offset lingering fiscal anxieties. The MSCI World Index climbed to 4,986.16 by the end of July 2026, while gold surged past $4,504.10/oz on USD weakness and central bank demand. Meanwhile, Brent crude held steady near $88.29/bbl amid Middle East risk premiums, and global bond markets remain bifurcated, with shorter-dated yields softening on rate-cut expectations even as the US 30-year yield recently touched 5.34% on structural debt concerns.
As US growth investors, we are laser-focused on how this macro tape intersects with our core holdings. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 closed July 2026 at 7,711.76 and 29,433.43, respectively, reflecting a market that is pricing in a flawless AI-driven earnings expansion. The S&P 500 trailing P/E ratio sits at 29.72 as of 31 July 2026. While not quite the stratospheric 39x seen in early 2021, it closely mirrors the ~30x multiple of mid-1999. Back then, a secular technological shift justified premium valuations for a select group of winners, much like today’s AI capex boom. However, looking under the hood, the current tape shares eerie similarities with the late-cycle environments of 1999 and 2007, where late-stage euphoria masks underlying structural fractures.



Performance of Major US Stock Indices


The bond market is flashing a critical warning that equity markets are currently ignoring. The 10-year yield at 4.68% and the 30-year yield at 5.34% reflect a structural US fiscal deficit of $1.8 trillion and a national debt exceeding $40 trillion. More importantly, the 2Y/10Y yield spread has un-inverted to +47.5 bps as of 31 July 2026. Historically, the steepening of the yield curve after a prolonged inversion has been a highly reliable precursor to recession, signaling that the Fed’s tightening has finally broken something in the real economy. We saw this exact dynamic in early 2001 and late 2007, where the curve steepened just months before severe equity drawdowns.



US 2Y and 10Y Treasury Yields and Spread


The real economy is showing distinct late-cycle fatigue, further validating the bond market’s caution. Unemployment ticked up to 4.1% in July 2026, while Q2 GDP growth slowed to a 1.5% annualized pace. This combination of decelerating growth and rising joblessness mirrors the mid-2000 to early-2001 period, where the Fed paused but the technology and manufacturing sectors were already rolling over. Furthermore, household debt service payments sit at 11.16% of disposable income as of Q1 2026, squeezing the consumer and making the economy heavily reliant on the wealth effect from equity markets rather than organic wage growth.



US Unemployment Rate


Navigating this environment requires separating the secular growth trends from the cyclical macro headwinds. The recent Jackson Hole symposium was deemed hawkish but tolerable, and the VIX remains benign at 14.43 as of 31 July 2026, indicating deep market complacency. To position for the months ahead, we must weigh the structural risks against the pockets of undeniable opportunity.

Fiscal Dominance and Bond Vigilantes: The structural US fiscal deficit is pushing long-end yields higher regardless of Fed policy. If the 10-year yield breaches 5.0% sustainably, it will severely compress the duration-adjusted valuations of long-term growth stocks, much like the 2000 yield spike triggered the dot-com unwind.
Yield Curve Un-inversion Recession Signal: The historical precedent of the 2Y/10Y curve steepening after a deep inversion typically precedes a credit event or recession by 6 to 12 months. With high-yield OAS spreads currently at a complacent 2.85% as of 31 July 2026, the credit market is not pricing in the stress that the bond market’s long end is warning about.
Quality and Free Cash Flow Compounders: In a late-cycle environment where GDP is slowing to 1.5% and unemployment is rising to 4.1%, growth stocks with fortress balance sheets and pricing power will decouple from the broader market. The recent rotation into “Quality” and “Value” factors in July 2026 highlights a market beginning to demand actual cash flows over speculative AI promises.
Short-Duration and Financial Beneficiaries: With the Fed Funds rate at 3.75% and the front-end of the curve softening, financials and highly levered but cash-flow-positive tech firms can benefit from expanding net interest margins if the curve continues to steepen, offering a hedge against long-end volatility.




MSCI World Equity Index



Suggested Portfolio Exposure: 50-75%
Justification: We are in the twilight of the current credit cycle. The AI-driven earnings growth is real and provides a cushion against moderate valuation compression, but the macro underpinnings—rising unemployment, fiscal deficits, and a steepening yield curve—scream late-cycle. Maintaining a 50-75% exposure allows us to capture the remaining upside of the secular AI growth theme while preserving enough dry powder to deploy into deep value or defensive growth if the yield curve’s recession signal materializes into a broader credit event. We must be highly selective, favoring profitable growth over speculative duration, and recognize that the easy money of the zero-interest-rate era is permanently behind us.

title: About
text:
This project combines historical and real-time financial data with AI to produce automated research reports for US growth stock investors. By feeding macroeconomic indicators, equity market data, and commodity prices into an AI model, each report identifies historical patterns, draws parallels to current conditions, and highlights risks and opportunities for growth-oriented portfolios.
All charts and visualizations in the reports are created by the author — the AI generates only the written analysis.

Data Sources
Every report is grounded in real data from:

FRED (Federal Reserve Economic Data): Inflation (CPI), GDP growth, unemployment, Fed balance sheet, Treasury yields, household debt, recession indicators, Fed funds rate, and high-yield credit spreads
Yahoo Finance: MSCI World Index, S&P 500, NASDAQ 100, Dow Jones, VIX, gold, and Brent crude oil
Multpl.com: S&P 500 trailing P/E ratios
